title: Flatness-Aware Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics
claim: Performance peaks and stays stable inside the theoretically prescribed noise–temperature coupling regime, and degrades sharply when the parameters are decoupled.
layout: 2 vertically stacked line plots, dual x-axes, shaded theory regime band
description: Two vertically stacked line plots with accuracy on the y-axis. Each plot has two x-axes. The bottom axis shows the varied hyperparameter on a log scale: σ in (a) and β in (b). The top axis shows the implied exponent η, running from -1 to 3 in (a) and from -2 to 3 in (b). A pale blue shaded band marks η between 0 and 1 and is labeled 'Theoretical β-σ coupling regime'. In (a), β is fixed at 10^8. The top part of the plot is a broken-axis zoom with error bars, where accuracy sits near 91.5 inside the band and drops to about 91 outside it. The small lower segment shows accuracy collapsing to between about 10 and 75 at large σ. In (b), σ is fixed at 10^-3. Accuracy is a flat plateau near 90 across the shaded band and falls steeply on both sides. Captions sit below each panel. The eye goes first to the blue line and the highlighted band.
caption: Performance of fSGLD as a function of the implied exponent η, where η is computed from the coupling σ = β−(1+η)/4. Top: fixing β and varying σ. Bottom: fixing σ and varying β. The bottom x-axis corresponds to the varied parameter (σ or β), while the top x-axis shows the implied exponent η.
abstract: Flatness of the loss landscape has been widely studied as an important perspective for understanding the behavior and generalization of deep learning algorithms. Motivated by this view, we propose Flatness-Aware Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (fSGLD), a first-order optimization method that biases learning its dynamics toward flat basins while retaining the computational and memory efficiency of SGD and SGLD. We provide a non-asymptotic theoretical analysis showing that fSGLD targets a flatness-biased Gibbs distribution under a theoretically prescribed coupling between the noise scale $Ï$ and the inverse temperature $Î²$, together with explicit excess risk guarantees. We empirically evaluate fSGLD across standard optimizer benchmarks, Bayesian image classification, uncertainty quantification, and out-of-distribution detection, demonstrating consistently strong performance and reliable uncertainty estimates. Additional experiments confirm the effectiveness of the theoretically prescribed $Î²$-$Ï$ coupling compared to decoupled choices.
